The point of something like Depression Quest isn't to make you want to play more- the point of the options that you can't take is to show that depression takes these away from people. Was it perfect? No. Did it get the point across? Absolutely.

Chasing the Manic Pixie Dream Girl is a free, public domain browser game- it's literally about coming to terms with a girl not being interested in you. How is that a bad thing, exactly? I haven't played it, and frankly, I don't care to, but I think it sounds fascinatingly subversive. A dating sim in which you win by giving up on the girl? I don't think that's hurting anybody.

"This woman's looked at gaming culture and seen fit to compare it to a zombie apocalypse." Well, no crap. People sent death threats to the developers of No Man's Sky when they announced that the game would be delayed.

Games that are intentionally preachy, like any art that's made preachy, isn't going to be very good. Many of the games in this video were weak examples of diverse games. There's nothing wrong with using your art to send a message, but when your message trumps everything else, your art suffers, and I feel like that's the case for this video. This is peak cherrypicking.

That said, I do feel that he made a good point towards the end: "Message gets first priority and the medium is trampled on to accommodate it, sacrificing everything that creating a game, instead of something else, makes sense in the first place. Why does that matter? It can be incredibly frustrating when you're playing them. To experience such a seemingly unavoidable trainwreck... It suggests games must not be quite as vulnerable to certain kinds of ideological injection as other media is. Gameplay gets in the way as a creative barrier to anyone who's just in it to throw their story at a new audience."

What he said at the very end struck me as particularly stupid, however- I don't think that the point of the Depression Quests and Autism Simulators and what have you is to change gaming as a whole- I think it's just to bring certain issues to light, and I don't think that there's anything wrong with that. I would like to see better-made protest games, and games that do a better job at bringing attention to issues, and you know what?

They do exist.

Look at 1979 Revolution, a game about the revolution in Iran- it's a well-made adventure, and it was just banned in Iran. That's a very "diverse" game. Why didn't this guy talk about games like that?
